smell: Orchestrator.Run returns immediately when a fatal step fails. In destroy, StepDestroyInfra defaults to Fatal=true, so if `terraform destroy` fails the orchestrator skips StepRemoveRemoteISO, StepCleanupFiles, StepCleanupFirewall, and StepPrintSummary — leaving a half-destroyed cluster with no firewall cleanup, stale ISOs, haproxy/dnsmasq still running, and no summary. The OnError hook even prints 'file cleanup will be skipped unless --force is used' (destroy/steps.go:40) but `Force` is hard-coded to true in okd.Provisioner.Destroy (okd.go:152) and is not threaded into the orchestrator's continue-past-fatal decision anywhere.
severity_reason: Data-loss-adjacent: partial-destroy state where user thinks tool gave up but actually never attempted the 4 follow-up cleanup steps. Not blocker because cluster is not destroyed and user can re-run; but rubric §4/canonical-helper-on-critical-path applies — destroy path.
fix_summary: Either (a) make StepDestroyInfra NonFatal=true when opts.Force is set so downstream cleanup always runs, tracking TF failure via a phase-context flag that StepPrintSummary can surface; or (b) add a Continue-On-Fatal hook interface so Force mode flows the error back to the user while still running cleanup. The per-step Fatal boolean + orchestrator's early-return is coarse-grained for this use case.
rule_source: CLAUDE.md §architecture-notes (canonical BuildSteps/Fatal semantics)
repo-counter-example: internal/distribution/okd/destroy/steps.go:39-42 (OnError text already contemplates a 'force continues' semantic that code doesn't implement)
must_preserve: StepDef/BuildSteps canonical API; do not introduce a second orchestration framework

smell: destroyWithPlan falls back to destroyDirect (terraform destroy -auto-approve) if `terraform plan -destroy` fails. Plan failures typically indicate a real problem (provider auth, malformed state, backend lock). Silently promoting a plan failure to an unplanned auto-approved destroy removes the preview safety gate and can destroy resources the operator never saw listed. The fallback makes UsePlan: true effectively equivalent to UsePlan: false whenever the plan side errors.
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss — destroy-without-plan is silently substituted for destroy-with-plan on plan error, subverting the documented 'safer plan-then-apply approach' (destroy/helpers.go:40).
fix_summary: Return the plan error instead of falling back. If callers want destroyDirect semantics they can set UsePlan: false explicitly. Alternatively, require an explicit 'AllowUnplannedFallback' opt — defaulting to false. Remove the misleading 'safer plan-then-apply approach' comment in destroy/helpers.go:40 until the fallback is removed or gated.
rule_source: CLAUDE.md §security-invariants (destroy ordering)
Terraform docs: 'Use plans for review before apply'
repo-counter-example: internal/distribution/okd/destroy/helpers.go:37-41 (`UsePlan: true // use safer plan-then-apply approach`)

smell: destroy has no --dry-run / --plan flag. The only pre-destroy safety is a single y/N prompt, bypassable by --force / -y. An operator cannot see 'here is what would be destroyed' before committing. Roadmap item M3 (not started) tracks this as an explicit gap for deploy/destroy/update-ingress. Deploy has the same gap.
evidence:
destroyCmd.Flags().BoolVarP(&destroyForce, "force", "y", false, "skip confirmation prompt")
destroyCmd.Flags().BoolVar(&destroyKeepISOs, "keep-isos", false, "do not remove the FCOS ISO from the Proxmox host")
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss — a destructive command with no preview mode is a standard foot-gun; mitigated by y/N prompt but only one layer deep.
fix_summary: Add --dry-run (or --plan) that: (a) skips the sudo re-exec, (b) runs `terraform plan -destroy` and prints the plan, (c) lists every mutating step the destroy orchestrator *would* run, (d) exits 0 on success / 2 on plan failure (matches U4 errtypes). Wire equivalent on deploy and update-ingress for symmetry.
rule_source: roadmap.md M3 (acceptance: --dry-run on deploy/destroy/update-ingress)
CWE-710 (Improper adherence to coding standards: destructive command without preview)
must_preserve: the existing y/N prompt; the --force / -y flag

smell: StepDestroyInfra.OnError warns 'file cleanup will be skipped unless --force is used', implying that setting Force=true will let cleanup continue. But `okd.Provisioner.Destroy` always sets `destroyOpts.Force = true` (okd.go:152) and the orchestrator's fatal-step handling (orchestrator.go:56) doesn't read Force at all — on TF failure the orchestrator always returns early, cleanup always skipped. The warning is permanently a lie in the current call graph.
severity_reason: This is a log-text correctness bug — it misleads the operator into thinking a knob exists that would change behavior. Not data-loss, but erodes trust in diagnostic output. Fix is either implement the semantic (see state:366b3f2d:fatal-step-blocks-cleanup) or change the message to match current reality.
fix_summary: Either: (a) implement the semantic — make StepDestroyInfra NonFatal when Force is set so cleanup follows, or (b) remove the `if !opts.Force` conditional and print a plain 'file cleanup skipped — run `okdctl cleanup` manually to finish teardown'. Option (b) is a 2-line fix, Option (a) is the real fix.
rule_source: CLAUDE.md §error-messages
Go proverb: 'errors are values — errors tell the operator what to do'

smell: okdctl.yaml has no schemaVersion / apiVersion field. Loader.LoadFile uses sigs.k8s.io/yaml (Unmarshal without DisallowUnknownFields), so a config authored for an old binary silently accepts fields the new binary removed, and a config authored for a new binary silently drops fields the old binary doesn't recognise. There is no migration path, no 'this config was written by version X' marker, no fail-closed behavior on version skew. A user who bumps okdctl and re-runs destroy on a stale config can trigger surprising behavior with no diagnostic.
severity_reason: Non-obvious correctness risk: config schema drift silently mis-behaves destroy/deploy on upgrades. Becomes blocker once config semantics change between versions (e.g. a field is renamed or removed).
fix_summary: Add `schemaVersion string` to Config (top-level, json:"schema_version"). Defaults inject current version. Loader validates: reject if major > binary's supported; warn if minor differs; reject unknown fields via sigs.k8s.io/yaml.UnmarshalStrict (or Decoder.KnownFields(true) if migrating to yaml.v3). Write a migration registry keyed by from-version for future field moves.
rule_source: Kubernetes resource apiVersion convention
repo-counter-example: internal/distribution/okd/postinstall/update_ingress.go:454 sets `APIVersion: "operator.openshift.io/v1"` on generated k8s objects — same pattern applies here
must_preserve: existing DefaultConfig + sigs.k8s.io/yaml roundtrip; json tags are authoritative per types.go:8

smell: Two concurrent `okdctl deploy` or `okdctl destroy` invocations in the same project root both point at `infrastructure/terraform/environments/<env>/terraform.tfstate` with no Go-side barrier. Terraform itself takes a local-backend lock only around individual sub-commands (init/plan/apply/destroy each relock), so a race between okdctl run A's plan step and run B's destroy step is not protected end-to-end. Nothing in okdctl's own orchestrator checks 'am I the only okdctl running?' — no pidfile, no flock, no stale-run detection.
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss — concurrent runs on the same state file can interleave at any terraform command boundary and corrupt state. Mitigated by single-operator discipline but not enforced.
fix_summary: Acquire a flock on `<workDir>/.okdctl.lock` at orchestrator entry (deploy/destroy/cleanup/update-ingress). Release on orchestrator exit. On contention, fail fast with 'another okdctl run is active (pid=N, started=T)' instead of racing. Use `github.com/gofrs/flock` (BSD-licensed, no transitive weight). The lock is orthogonal to terraform's own lock — it prevents two okdctl orchestrators from interleaving at step boundaries.
rule_source: Terraform local-backend docs (per-command lock, not per-orchestration lock)
Go proverb: 'do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating' — single-writer invariant
must_preserve: existing terraform.Executor API; single-operator usage pattern

smell: StepDef has no 'already-done' precondition hook or checkpoint. If okdctl crashes mid-setup (e.g. after building ISOs but before uploading), the next run starts from step 1, repeating work or reconciling side-effects ad-hoc. Each step's idempotency is implicit — some steps check FileExists (setup/artifacts.go:110), others re-run unconditionally (GenerateManifests, Inject*). There is no declared `ReRunSafe bool` field on StepDef and no on-disk checkpoint recording 'last-completed-step-id' that the next orchestrator run can skip to. InterruptSummary (cli/summary.go:163) tells the user 'resume with okdctl deploy' but the resume simply re-runs from step 0.
evidence:
type StepDef struct {
    ID         StepID
    Name       string
    Desc       string
    NonFatal   bool
    SkipWhen   func() bool
    SkipReason string
    OnStart    func()
    Exec       func(ctx context.Context) error
    OnError    func(error)
}
severity_reason: Not blocker — re-running deploy is mostly harmless because most steps happen to be idempotent, but the implicit-idempotency contract is fragile. Upgrades to the 40-step phase graph risk introducing a non-idempotent step that silently corrupts a partial deploy.
fix_summary: Option A (lightweight): add `ReRunSafe bool` on StepDef, default false, and require every StepDef to declare it (compile-fail via lint if a step sets Fatal without setting ReRunSafe explicitly). Document the contract in step.go. Option B (heavier): add on-disk checkpoint at `<workDir>/.okdctl-progress.json` — StepResult list after each step, skipped on re-run when step.ID matches. Start with A — cheap, forces authors to think about idempotency at the StepDef level.
rule_source: CLAUDE.md §architecture-notes (StepDef + BuildSteps canonical API)
Twelve-factor §disposability (processes should be resilient to crashes)
repo-counter-example: roadmap.md mentions N10 'Ctrl-C partial-progress summary' shipped but no resume semantic
must_preserve: StepDef + BuildSteps canonical API; backward compat for existing StepDefs

smell: destroySteps is all-or-nothing. Options expose SkipTerraform / SkipCleanup / SkipFirewall / KeepISOs as separate booleans, but there is no user-facing CLI flag to scope — `okdctl destroy` always runs the full graph. Operators who want 'destroy only VMs but keep haproxy/dnsmasq/firewall for debug' or 'destroy only files, infra is already gone' cannot express that without editing code or running `okdctl cleanup` as a separate command (which has its own issues — cleanup.Execute covers Full / WorkOnly / WebOnly / HAProxyOnly / TerraformOnly but destroy doesn't thread a --scope flag to it).
severity_reason: Feature-gap, not correctness. Workaround exists (run `okdctl cleanup` with its richer Kind enum). The destroy-side scoping just isn't exposed.
fix_summary: Add --scope=full|infra|files|firewall (default: full) and --skip-firewall / --skip-cleanup flags on destroyCmd, routing to the existing Options fields. Promote the cleanup.Kind enum so destroyCmd can accept the same scope names users already know from `okdctl cleanup`.
rule_source: roadmap.md N4 (okdctl cleanup standalone) demonstrates scoped teardown works; destroy should match its vocabulary
must_preserve: default behavior (full destroy on no flag)

smell: CleanupBootstrap creates `bootstrap-destroy.tfplan` via tf.Plan, then applies it, and only calls SafeRemove on the plan file on the success path. If tf.Apply fails, the plan file persists in the terraform dir. terraform.Executor.Cleanup (terraform.go:302) removes only `tfplan` / `destroy.tfplan` / `terraform.tfstate.backup` — not `bootstrap-destroy.tfplan`. A subsequent re-run of postinstall will plan again and overwrite the stale file, but a following `terraform` CLI inspection by the operator sees a stale plan that doesn't match current state.
severity_reason: Low-impact — a stray `bootstrap-destroy.tfplan` doesn't corrupt anything and next run overwrites it. Logged as a recovery hygiene issue, not a safety one.
fix_summary: Use `defer system.SafeRemove(planPath)` right after tf.Plan succeeds so the plan is removed regardless of Apply outcome. Or add 'bootstrap-destroy.tfplan' to terraform.Executor.Cleanup's file list.
rule_source: repo-counter-example: internal/infrastructure/terraform/terraform.go:302-313 already centralizes plan cleanup

smell: StepPrintSummary logs 'destroy: cluster teardown completed' unconditionally at end of the pipeline. If any upstream NonFatal step failed (remove-remote-iso, cleanup-files, cleanup-firewall), the summary still announces completion. Operator reading logs thinks 'we're clean' when firewall rules and ISOs may still be present on disk/firewalld. StepResult slice in orchestrator.Results() has the truth, but the summary step doesn't inspect it — it just prints a fixed string.
severity_reason: Observability gap in a destructive-op summary. Not blocker because the underlying Warn logs from failed sub-steps are still emitted — the operator has signal, just buried.
fix_summary: Have StepPrintSummary inspect orchestrator.Results() (or accept a PhaseContext with step outcomes) and render the same structured box summary.InterruptSummary uses — one row per step with ok/fail/skip status. If any step failed, emit 'destroy: teardown completed with N warning(s); see log above' instead of an unconditional success line.
rule_source: repo-counter-example: internal/cli/summary.go:160-192 already has the pattern for per-step ok/fail rendering

smell: postinstall steps (cleanup-bootstrap, deploy-production-dns) are NonFatal and mutate cluster-external state (bootstrap VM destroyed via targeted tf apply, /etc/dnsmasq.d/*.conf replaced). If StepCleanupBootstrap succeeds but StepVerifyKubeVIP fails and StepDeployProductionDNS is skipped, the cluster is left with: bootstrap VM gone, kube-vip not verified, DNS still pointed at bootstrap. The user has no resume command specific to 'just the postinstall DNS step'. The destroy path will cope, but an operator trying to recover a stuck deploy has to hand-edit dnsmasq configs or re-run full deploy.
severity_reason: Design debt not correctness bug: the staged NonFatal approach is intentional (degrade-gracefully to haproxy routing when kube-vip fails) but the resume story for 'finish postinstall DNS when kube-vip comes up later' is not documented and has no dedicated CLI path. `okdctl update-ingress` covers a different scenario.
fix_summary: Two options: (a) add `okdctl postinstall --step=dns` subcommand that re-runs just the DNS sub-phase once kube-vip is confirmed healthy; or (b) expand update-ingress to handle the bootstrap→production DNS transition when it's still pointing at bootstrap IP. Prefer (b) since update-ingress already owns DNS re-deploys.
rule_source: CLAUDE.md §architecture-notes (phase idempotency expectation)
repo-counter-example: internal/distribution/okd/postinstall/update_ingress.go already re-deploys DNS
must_preserve: postinstall step ordering; NonFatal semantics that let partial success still give a usable cluster

smell: Provider.Provision delegates 100% to terraform — no Go-side retry on transient Proxmox API failures, no 409-already-exists handling beyond what the bpg/proxmox provider does internally. retrieveProvisionResult (proxmox.go:187) derives VM IPs from config (not from Proxmox), so eventual-consistency 'VM created but not yet listed' gaps are dodged by not querying Proxmox — but any future code that enumerates VMs from the API will need retry. The comment at proxmox.go:160 'run okdctl destroy to clean up' is the only recovery guidance on apply failure.
severity_reason: Currently no direct Proxmox API calls from Go (the provider is pure-terraform), so there's nothing to retry. Filed as a forward-looking note for when any future code paths query Proxmox directly (e.g. status checks that don't go through terraform output).
fix_summary: Document the invariant in proxmox.go header: 'All Proxmox mutation MUST go through terraform.Executor. Direct HTTP calls are forbidden.' If/when status queries are added, use internal/download's retry helper (5xx/408/429 with exponential backoff, 4xx fail-fast) which is already justified for HTTP retries.
rule_source: repo-counter-example: internal/download/retry.go (established retry pattern in repo per roadmap U3)

smell: Config types use sigs.k8s.io/yaml which silently drops unknown fields by default. No call in the codebase uses a 'strict' or 'UnmarshalStrict' variant. A typo like `topolog: {...}` (missing 'y') is silently ignored; the user gets default topology and destroy/deploy behaves on defaults without warning. Strict mode would turn that into a load error.
severity_reason: Config typos silently accepted is a known foot-gun; mitigated by DefaultConfig being sane and by the config having many required-ish fields that validators catch. Upgrading to strict mode is a small fix with proportional payoff.
fix_summary: Swap `yaml.Unmarshal(data, cfg)` for `yaml.UnmarshalStrict(data, cfg)` in loader.go:LoadFile. Add a test that asserts a bogus field errors. Expect some churn if any configs in the wild use legacy fields — migrate via schemaVersion first (see state:a55b4592:no-schema-version).
rule_source: sigs.k8s.io/yaml docs: UnmarshalStrict rejects unknown fields
